title: Opportunistic KV reservation and soft-start model ladder for graceful OOM recovery
creator: Priya Nambiar
description: Problem: GPU OOMs during continuous batching remain a top cause of degraded tail latency and partial responses. Existing heuristics (hard slab eviction, reactive spill) either cause noisy retries or large fidelity drops. This ticket proposes two coordinated runtime mechanisms: 1) an opportunistic KV reservation that budgets a small, reclaimable token-sized reservation per active request (no global slab allocations), and 2) a soft-start model ladder that opportunistically serves an initial token stream with a compact or quantized variant and promotes to the full model only when memory headroom and KV state are available. Together these aim to reduce hard OOMs and preference smooth degradation instead of abrupt failures.
background: We see recurring incidents where a burst of concurrent streaming requests with long contexts saturates KV memory during continuous batching windows. Current fallback strategies often evict entire segments or switch to much smaller models mid-response, causing poor UX and follow-up retries. Recent infra experiments suggest smaller, reclaimable reservations and incremental model promotion reduce OOM frequency and reduce retries by up to 30% (internal experiment #2026-02-batch-sim). This ticket encodes the feature design and rollout plan.
goals:
- Prevent catastrophic OOMs for common burst patterns while preserving overall throughput.
- Provide predictable, observable behavior for callers (clear degradation path and retry semantics).
- Allow config tuning per-customer/route (reservation budget, ladder tiers).
- Keep token-cost overhead minimal (<1% typical).
non_goals: - This work does not replace long-term kernel-level memory compaction or host-spill solutions. It is an application-layer mitigation to buy time/latency headroom and smooth degradation.
proposed_design:
Core components:
1) Opportunistic KV Reservation (OKR): each incoming request creates a small reclaimable reservation object expressed as token_count (default 64 tokens). Reservations are 'soft' — they mark an anticipated KV allocation but do not immediately materialize full KV pages.
2) Batch Shepherd: admission controller that uses OKR aggregate to decide whether to allow a request into the current continuous-batching window or place it into a short waiting queue (micro-shepherd queue) to avoid bursts.
3) Soft-Start Model Ladder: requests begin on a compact execution path (quantized/half-precision micro-model or a short-context compressor) that emits first tokens using minimal KV; if the OKR is satisfied for the next N tokens, the runtime promotes the request to the full model and realizes the KV pages. Promotion is stepwise and reversible (demote if contention rises).
4) Tumble Recovery Orchestrator: when an OOM or near-OOM is detected, mark affected GPUs with a short 'tumble' cooldown where new admissions use the ladder default micro-model and existing KV reservations are compacted. The orchestrator coordinates across replicas to avoid simultaneous heavy promotions.
work_items: Add micro-shepherd admission queue and policy hooks
Integrate ladder-aware execution paths in runtime kernel selection
Promotion/demotion safe points and checkpointing for KV realization
Tumble cooldown state machine and cluster coordination
Add observability (reservation gauge, promotion rate, demotion/retry counters)
E2E regression tests with bursty streaming workloads
tradeoffs_and_risks:
- Reservation sizing: too small yields no benefit; too large wastes GPU memory. We will start conservative (64 tokens) and tune via prod experiments.
- Additional complexity in runtime & scheduling; potential for new bugs in promotion/demotion logic.
- Slight increase in per-request latency on paths that start micro-model first (expected <5ms).
- Risk of cascading promotions if many requests simultaneously find headroom; mitigated by Batch Shepherd global window cap.
rollout_plan:
Phase 1 (canary): enable OKR+shepherd+ladder on a small fleet (10% runtime nodes) and a single non-critical route. Monitor reservation utilization and promotion success.
Phase 2 (beta): expand to 40% with tunable per-customer flags and alert thresholds.
Phase 3 (wide): default enable on runtime-2.3 where metrics show reduced OOM rate and acceptable latency.
Fallback: full rollback via runtime flag to disable OKR+ladder quickly.
acceptance_criteria:
- OOM incidents (GPU OOMs) reduce by >=40% on canary route compared to baseline bursts.
- Promotion success rate >=90% (promoted requests complete without demotion).
- Median latency change <= +3ms; p95 increase <= +10ms.
- No increase in client-visible partial responses.
- Metrics and dashboards available: reservation_gauge, promotion_rate, demotion_rate, shepherd_enqueue_count.
testing_plan: Unit tests for reservation allocator; integration test for promotion/demotion checkpointing; synthetic load tests: 1) burst of 300 concurrent streaming requests with 8k context, 2) mixed priority workloads with tail-heavy contexts. Chaos tests: inject OOM at kernel layer to validate tumble orchestrator and safe rollback. Run A/B for 2 weeks on beta fleet.
metrics:
- GPU OOM count per node per hour
- Reservation utilization ratio (used / reserved)
- Promotion success rate
- Average time-to-promotion (ms)
- Shepherd queue wait time distribution
- Retry rate from callers
- End-to-end success rate
